cases.title: Nis railway bypass: a block of flats marked for demolition, six families bought out and an eviction petition
cases.point: Nis city centre (approximate). The Complaints Mechanism gives no street or settlement name for the building.

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: The Board of Directors approved an investment loan of up to EUR 134 million on 1 December 2017 and a further EUR 100 million in July 2024. The borrower is the Republic of Serbia and the promoter is Serbian Railways Infrastructure.

lenders.name: Western Balkans Investment Framework
lenders.role: EUR 106 million in grants. The Complaints Mechanism's dispute resolution report of 5 November 2025 says the project receives "EUR 106 million grants from the Western Balkans Investment Framework". It gives no date for that support.

cases.conditions: The City of Nis and the promoter adopted a Resettlement Action Plan in October 2019. For the five remaining tenant families it set out tenant-purchase of their flats followed by entry into the expropriation procedure. The Complaints Mechanism records that "The arrangement foreseen in the RAP was not implemented."

companies.name: MIN Holding (Masinska industrija Nis)
companies.role: The dispute resolution report of 5 November 2025 describes MIN Holding as "Masinska industrija Nis (MIN Holding), a limited liability company which went bankrupt in 2015", and says the building "was owned by" it. The report does not say who owns the building now. MIN Holding filed the eviction petition against the complainant. It is a Serbian company, not an outside investor; it is listed here because it owned the building and brought the eviction.

cases.community: A resident of Nis complained to the EIB's Complaints Mechanism on 8 September 2022. The office's dispute resolution report of 5 November 2025 says: "The residential building in which the complainant lives is set to be demolished in order to complete the project." The report says the building "contains 16 units, of which five apartments were unoccupied". The rest were rented to former employees. Of the 11 tenant families, "six families regulated their relationship with MIN Holding" and "became owners of the respective apartments, received compensation and moved out". Five families, including the complainant, remained tenants. The City of Nis offered social housing, which the complainant rejected because the flat was smaller and the tenancy ran five years "with the possibility of an extension" while the existing tenancy was for an indefinite period. The report states: "MIN Holding filed an eviction petition against the complainant in September 2022." It says the complainant then "filed a court petition in October 2022 to grant them the right to purchase (tenant-purchase) the apartment". A second complaint, SG/E/2025/13, was received on 24 September 2025 from an employee of the promoter who lives with his wife and three children in a flat the promoter owns on the Stanicenje-Dimitrovgrad section; the initial assessment report of 10 March 2026 says "The apartment will need to be demolished for the Stanicenje-Dimitrovgrad component of the project" and records no demolition, eviction or rehousing having taken place.
cases.displaced_label: families who became owners of their flats, were compensated and moved out
cases.displaced_note: The dispute resolution report of 5 November 2025 says six of the 11 tenant families "regulated their relationship with MIN Holding" and "became owners of the respective apartments, received compensation and moved out". It does not give the dates or the amounts, and it does not say whether the building has been demolished. What the five remaining tenant families received is covered by the confidential settlement of September 2025.
cases.outcome: Dialogue ran from December 2022 to September 2025. The dispute resolution report says the facilitation team "conducted two rounds of joint dialogue sessions in May and December 2023" and "held numerous bilateral meetings with the parties", and names the City of Nis, the bankruptcy administrator of MIN Holding and the Serbian Bankruptcy Supervision Agency as important stakeholders. The parties "managed to reach a final settlement agreement in September 2025" and agreed to keep its content confidential. In January 2026 the promoter and the complainant "confirmed that they considered the agreement to be fully implemented", and the Complaints Mechanism reported on 16 January 2026 that it had ended its monitoring. The case page records the case as closed on 16 January 2026, the outcome as "Friendly solution" and suggestions for improvement as "N/A". The dispute resolution report says "The legal complexity of the case posed challenges", that "various ongoing parallel judicial proceedings had to be considered", and that "Parliamentary and municipal elections, changing leadership and a fatal accident at a train station in Novi Sad (that led to country-wide protests)" "negatively impacted the parties' focus on the dispute resolution process". The second complaint on the Stanicenje-Dimitrovgrad section is to go to collaborative dispute resolution.

cases.confidence_note: Nothing here is disputed by the lender or by any other source. It is marked contested because the core harm rests on a single document: the EIB Complaints Mechanism's dispute resolution report of 5 November 2025. That report is the lender's own factual record, not the complainant's allegation, and I opened it and checked each figure in it. It records the building as "set to be demolished", not demolished, and does not say whether the building has since come down or whether the complainant's household moved or was rehoused. The six families who moved out, the eviction petition of September 2022 and the sentence "The arrangement foreseen in the RAP was not implemented" are all in that report. No date or amount is given for the six families' compensation. The September 2025 settlement is confidential by agreement, so what the five remaining families received is not public, and a settlement is not an admission of liability. The report gives no date for the EUR 106 million in Western Balkans Investment Framework grants. The building is in Nis but no street is named, so the point is the city.

cases.title: Bogota Metro Line 1: 1,264 buildings demolished along the route
cases.place: First Line of the Bogota Metro, Bosa to Calle 72, Bogota, Colombia
cases.point: Avenida Caracas at Calle 26, a point on the Line 1 alignment (approximate). The demolitions run the length of the 24 km route through Bosa, Kennedy, Puente Aranda, Los Martires, Antonio Narino, Santa Fe, Chapinero, Teusaquillo and Barrios Unidos.

lenders.name: European Investment Bank (EIB)
lenders.role: The EIB Complaints Mechanism's initial assessment report of 19 November 2025 says that on 17 July 2018 the EIB "approved financing of Bogota Sustainable Transport Framework Loan (FL) in Colombia in the amount of up to USD 480m". It says "A first tranche of the EIB loan was signed on 6 August 2018 in the amount of USD 56m and a second, signed on 8 May 2023 in the amount of USD 50m", and that "As of the issuance of this report, the first tranche of USD 56m has been disbursed". Footnote 4 says "The first tranche relates to Bogota Metro Line 1, while the second relates to Bogota Metro Line 2." The same report also says that "On 5 February 2025, the EIB approved financing of Metro Line One". It puts the total project cost at USD 4.3 billion. The project is developed by Empresa Metro de Bogota SA, "a public company fully owned by the municipality of Bogota".

lenders.name: Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)
lenders.role: Section 1.5 of the EIB Complaints Mechanism's initial assessment report of 19 November 2025 says the project "will be partly financed by further loans from the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB)" and the IBRD. The wording is future, and the report gives no amounts. The city government said on 17 September 2025 that funds from the IDB and the World Bank were approved and would be disbursed before January 2026, which is after the demolitions counted to 28 February 2023. The IDB's Environmental and Social Grievance Protocol "is actively involved in a grievance-handling process with the complainant", and the EIB office informed the IDB's Independent Consultation and Investigation Mechanism of the complaint.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Named in the same sentence of the same report: the project "will be partly financed by further loans from" the IDB "and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD, part of the World Bank Group)". The wording is future and no amount is given. The EIB office informed the World Bank Inspection Panel of the complaint's registration. The city government named the World Bank alongside the IDB in its announcement of 17 September 2025.

cases.conditions: Property acquisition and relocation for Line 1 were carried out under the project's Resettlement Plan. The EIB complaint turns on whether shopkeepers along Calle 72 who were not expropriated should have been covered by it: the complainant says affected business owners along Calle 72 "have been excluded" from the Resettlement Action Plan, and the initial assessment report does not state whether that claim is valid.

companies.name: Metro Linea 1 S.A.S (ML1)
companies.role: Concessionaire responsible for the design, construction, operation and maintenance of Metro Line 1, per the EIB Complaints Mechanism (2025). Its owners are not named in any document I opened, so no headquarters is given here.

cases.community: The Bogota city government published figures on 29 March 2023, current to 28 February 2023. The acquisition target for Line 1 was 1,427 properties ("contempla la adquisicion de 1.427 predios"); 1,373 had been received ("ya se han recibido 1.373") and 54 were outstanding ("solo faltan 54 propiedades"), which the Empresa Metro de Bogota put at 96.3 per cent ("llevamos el 96.3% de predios adquiridos"). The city wrote: "Asimismo, se han demolido 1.264 construcciones a lo largo del trazado, cercanas al 89% del total" - 1,264 buildings demolished along the route, close to 89 per cent of the total. "1.046 predios estan entregados al concesionario". Of the 54 still outstanding, 19 had a promise of sale or an expropriation resolution, 24 were in notification and acceptance of an offer, and 11 were in the offer process. The manager of the Empresa Metro de Bogota, Leonidas Narvaez, said the acquisition "nos ha significado una inversion a pesos corrientes de 1,05 billones de pesos" - about 1.05 trillion current pesos, including social compensation. He said "hemos pagado las compensaciones sociales a las personas que hemos tenido que reubicar" - social compensation was paid to the people who had to be relocated - but the article gives no number of households or businesses and no amounts. The route "atraviesa las localidades de Bosa, Kennedy, Puente Aranda, Los Martires, Antonio Narino, Santa Fe, Chapinero, Teusaquillo y Barrios Unidos". Separately, a shop owner on Calle 72 complained to the EIB's Complaints Mechanism; its initial assessment report of 19 November 2025 says "the complainant alleges that project civil works have led to business disruptions", and records his account that road closures and congestion since May 2024 had cut customer access, reduced sales and profit, raised the risk of insolvency and led to staff dismissals. The office used the words "alleges" and "allegations", made no findings on the merits, and decided to carry out a compliance review.
cases.displaced_note: The city's figures count properties and demolished buildings, not households or businesses. The city says social compensation was paid to people who had to relocate but publishes no count of them in the article I read, so no displaced figure is given here.
cases.outcome: The Fraud Investigations Division of the Inspectorate General Directorate referred the shopkeeper's complaint to the Complaints Mechanism on 31 December 2024. It was deemed admissible on 14 February 2025 and registration was communicated to the complainant by email on 27 February 2025. An initial meeting with EIB services was held on 13 March 2025 and virtual calls with the complainant, the promoter and the concessionaire ran from March to July 2025. The office did not pursue dispute resolution: it says the test is "the willingness and interest of the parties" and "In this particular instance, this criterion has not been met". It says the parties "did express, at some point over the course of the initial assessment, a willingness and interest to engage" but "had markedly divergent views regarding the appropriate scope for the dialogue", which "ultimately led one party to express their preference for a compliance review"; the report does not say which party. The compliance review will cover the project's compliance with the EIB's environmental and social standards "including involuntary resettlement; and stakeholder engagement", and the office will liaise with the grievance services of the IDB and the IBRD. On 17 September 2025 the city said "Se trata del desembolso de 1.485 millones de dolares, equivalente a cerca de 5.7 billones de pesos" - a disbursement of USD 1,485 million, which it put at about 5.7 trillion pesos - and that "Los recursos ya estan aprobados y seran desembolsados antes de enero de 2026". That announcement names the World Bank and the IDB and does not mention the EIB.

cases.confidence_note: Marked contested because the harm rests on a single source. The property and demolition figures come only from the Bogota city government's own article of 29 March 2023, current to 28 February 2023, and that article does not mention the EIB, the IDB or the World Bank, so the outside-money link comes from a different document. The figures count properties and buildings, not people, so the number displaced is not known from them; the city says social compensation was paid to people who had to be relocated but publishes no count. The EIB's own dates do not sit together easily: the Complaints Mechanism report says the first tranche of USD 56 million was signed on 6 August 2018 and has been disbursed, with footnote 4 attaching that tranche to Metro Line 1, and the same report says the EIB approved financing of Metro Line One on 5 February 2025. No source I read explains the gap, and the explanation is unsourced. The IDB and the IBRD are named in the future tense - the project "will be partly financed by further loans from" them - with no amounts, and the city dated their approved funds to September 2025, after the demolitions counted here; the EIB tranche of 2018 is the financing that was in place while the properties were being taken. The shop owner's losses on Calle 72 are his allegations, recorded by the office, which had made no findings when I looked. The Early Warning System record for EIB-20220741 lists an investment of USD 430 million and a project cost of USD 5,789 million as at disclosure on 20 December 2024, which are different again from the report's figures; no source reconciles them.

lvwhy.project: The demolitions and property purchases were carried out to build the elevated metro line. The EIB's first tranche of USD 56 million, attached to Metro Line 1 by footnote 4 of its own office's report, was signed in August 2018 and had been disbursed.
lvwhy.land: 1,373 of a target of 1,427 properties had been received and 1,264 buildings demolished by 28 February 2023, with 19 of the remainder under a promise of sale or an expropriation resolution.

dropped.reason: Dropped on tests 2 and 3. The draft kept this on a land grant of about 700 hectares and on unpaid pasture and cabin compensation. I opened the single source that carries the harm, CEE Bankwatch Network's report of 11 September 2017 (https://bankwatch.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Nenskra-LALRP-11Sep2017.pdf), and it is written in the future and conditional throughout: "PAPs in these areas will be mainly affected by the temporary or permanent loss of pastures", a household "will be permanently affected by loss of pasture land and a wooden cabin at Mashrichala", "who will lose access to the Kvemo Memuli pasture area", and "these households would lose access" to cabins. Its field work was two visits, 1-5 and 17-19 July 2017, and 20 households. The draft had promoted these to completed losses, writing that access to cabins "is lost". The report says no compensation agreements had been signed - "This has not happened, but it is unclear what the new timeline is" - so there were offers outstanding for losses that had not yet occurred, not compensation owed for land people had already lost. The grant of 96.2 hectares in Chuberi for USD 1 and 600.0252 hectares for 55 years is a transfer on paper to the project company; nothing I opened records anyone losing the use of that land. The EIB Complaints Mechanism conclusions report of 7 February 2020 (https://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2018-32-nenskra-hpp-cr-3-06-2020-docx.pdf) does not state whether any land was transferred, acquired or occupied and does not state whether any compensation was paid, owed or withheld; the words LALRP, pastures, cabins and Kvemo Memuli do not appear in it. Its findings are about the Bank - no documented assessment under EIB Standard 7, "no evidence that the Bank took the adequate steps to assure itself of the proper application of Standard 7", an ADB vulnerability approach "very different from the definition of vulnerability in EIB Standard 7", a labour influx assessment "insufficient at this time" - and a finding against the lender is not harm. On timing: the NGO report to the Bern Convention of 12 February 2024 (https://rm.coe.int/files18e-2024-georgia-svaneti-nenskra-ngo-rep/1680aebea7) says "Local people informed us that work on none of the three projects has started yet" and "To the best of our knowledge, none has a construction company selected". Bankwatch's status update of 9 April 2020 (https://bankwatch.org/blog/status-update-on-the-nenskra-hydropower-plant-project) says activity "remains at a standstill", that the company abandoned the project "before construction had even begun", and that local sources said "almost all preparatory works have been stopped"; it records unpaid wages to local employees, not resident compensation. The EBRD IPAM case registry entry (https://www.ebrd.com/home/what-we-do/projects/independent-project-accountability-mechanism/case-registry/nenskra-hpp.html) gives a Monitoring Closing Report of 24 June 2026 stating "IPAM has been informed by Management that the Project has been cancelled" and that "the remaining open MAP actions are project-specific in nature", with obligations to be reactivated if the project is revived, materially restructured or resubmitted to the EBRD Board. So the project was cancelled before construction, and the preparation exception does not apply because no land take, tree felling, pasture loss or household move is documented anywhere I opened. ITEM I COULD NOT OPEN: business-humanrights.org's summary of an NGO report saying JSC Nenskra Hydro failed to compensate affected people. https://www.business-humanrights.org/en/latest-news/georgia-new-ngo-report-says-jsc-nenskra-hydro-fails-to-provide-adequate-compensation-for-people-affected-by-its-hydropower-plant-company-responds returned only site navigation and the headline, no body text; the French path https://business-humanrights.org/fr/dernieres-actualites/georgia-new-ngo-report-says-jsc-nenskra-hydro-fails-to-provide-adequate-compensation-for-people-affected-by-its-hydropower-plant-company-responds and https://www.bhrrc.org/ru/... both failed at the site with a client error. Neither is a host block. Searching for the underlying NGO report returned the same cluster of business-humanrights.org locale pages plus the 11 September 2017 Bankwatch report and its companion blog of the same date (https://bankwatch.org/blog/systematic-shortcomings-will-deprive-people-affected-by-georgian-dam-of-compensation), which I opened: it too says only that compensation "was offered" and "has been miscalculated", and describes cabins "that would be temporarily or permanently lost". That blog's own title is future tense. On the evidence I could reach, the business-humanrights item appears to summarise the 2017 Bankwatch report rather than a later one, so it would not add an independent source even if it opened. FIGURE PAIRS, for the record, each as its source states it and neither reconciled by anything I read: K-water's stake in JSC Nenskra Hydro is 85% per the EIB report of 7 February 2020, which gives no date label for the shareholding, and 80% per OC Media (2018); the EBRD is a 5% equity holder per that EIB report and a USD 214 million lender with a board date of 31 January 2018 and status "Approved" per the Early Warning System record for EBRD-46778. LENDER LIST, checked as asked: of the five institutions claimed, only two are documented as actually in. The EIB report puts the EIB's own loan of up to USD 150 million as approved on 6 February 2018 with status "Pending signature", and the 2024 NGO report says the EBRD and EIB loans of USD 214 million and USD 150 million "remain approved". The EIB report's footnote 1 names ADB, EBRD, KDB, AIIB and K-sure only as the "potential Lenders" as at November 2017, and the Early Warning System record for ADB-49223-001 lists the project as "Proposed". So ADB and AIIB are documented as potential or proposed only, and the draft's claim of five institutions on this project does not hold. K-water, 85% owner of the project company and itself 91.5% state-owned per the Early Warning System, is a real foreign owner, and the EBRD's 5% equity is real money in, so test 1 would pass; the case fails on tests 2 and 3. ALSO CORRECTED FROM THE DRAFT: the EBRD case page (https://www.ebrd.com/work-with-us/projects/ipam/2018/08.html) gives a registration date of 30 May 2018 with the Request document dated 11 June 2018, not a registration on 11 June 2018; the requesters are described as residents of four community members of Chuberi; and that page shows "Confidentiality Request: No" while its summary says they asked for their identities to be kept confidential, which the registry entry records as "Requested". The other agent working the ADB side of the same project dropped it too, so Nenskra now appears nowhere, and the one-case rule is satisfied.

Drop upheld, with one correction. I opened the case page (https://www.ebrd.com/work-with-us/projects/ipam/2020/07.html). The figure is not unsourced: the page itself says the requesters are "around 372 villagers" from Degirmenbasi, so 372 is the office's own approximate count of the people who complained. What is unsourced is the harm. The grazing loss appears only as the requesters' allegation - that mining is "adversely impacting the livelihoods of the community", that residents "can no longer depend on livestock breeding" because "the grazing lands have been taken by mine activities", and that promised vocational training and employment "have not materialised". The function requested was problem-solving only; the submission date is 23 August 2020, registration 21 December 2020, assessment report 2 March 2021, and the Problem Solving Completion Report of 7 September 2022 records the outcome as "No agreement reached". The page records no finding by the office on the merits and no documented loss of grazing land, and the requesters asked for confidentiality citing fear of retaliation, so there are no named plots or figures to check. The draft's account of the Early Warning System record for EBRD-49041 (USD 40 million, board date 29 November 2017, Lapseki and Ivrindi mines, no impacts or land acquisition recorded) and of a Turkish-language search returning only loan coverage stands as the writer recorded it; I did not re-run the search. Test 2 fails on an untested allegation.

Cut from the draft. Causation is not established for the house damage, and no document records land actually taken. I opened both monitoring reports. The final monitoring report for Chipambo and Geisha of 15 December 2022 (https://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2021-16a-chipambo-geisha-malawi-nrwb-water-efficiency-final-monitoring-report-2022-12-15.pdf) makes no finding on causation. It describes the promoter's approach as "to assess the damage to structures of the households concerned, evaluate the cost and then make the payment", and the payments as made under the promoter's "standing offer to pay", with no causal finding attached. In the one strand that was actually tested, the owner and the promoter jointly chose an independent engineer who found it "cannot be established" that the excavation works caused the damage, and both parties accepted that. Under the brief, a payment for assessed damage with no admission is a settlement without admission and does not establish the harm; here it is weaker still, because the only engineering test performed found against causation. The second monitoring report on Kazando of 15 March 2024 (https://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2021-16a-second-monitoring-report-kazando-malawi-nrwb-water-efficiency.pdf) likewise does not attribute the damage to the works: its only wording is "the damage to structures" and "the damaged structures in question". Neither report says any land was taken or occupied by the works. They record valuations and compensation payments - 234 households assessed, 231 signing on 6 July 2022, the finalised valuation report submitted by the Regional Commissioner for Lands North on 11 July 2022, 219 community members paid between 26 August and 21 September 2022 - but no description of land take, of what was lost, or of any amount. Compensation that was late and then paid is not documented harm; the writer dropped the Tunisian G1 Penetrante Sud lead on the same ground. TWO SOURCING ERRORS IN THE DRAFT, both corrected by reading the reports. First, the collapsed house: the report's wording is "One refused to receive payment because allegedly his house collapsed." That is the office's own sentence with the word "allegedly" in it, not the household's own statement as the draft said, and the draft quoted the clause with "allegedly" removed. Second, the draft said "The office's second monitoring report says the household counts of 13, 14, 15 and 17 differ across its own sections and does not reconcile them." The report says no such thing. It simply uses the different counts - "payment of the remaining compensation to 13 households", "the draft valuation report for the 14 missing households", "the Promoter made the payments to 15 households" with "Two households had already been paid previously", and "paid compensation to the 17 affected members of the community" - without reconciling them. The observation is the writer's, attributed to the office. The counts are accurate as quoted and the lack of reconciliation is real; there is a further unreconciled pair the draft missed, between the "two additional communal water points" in action 4 and the "request for additional three communal water points" in its status note. Other figures I checked and found accurate: the 20 of 38 paid on 13 December 2022, the assessment of 23 September to 3 October 2022 disclosed on 19 October 2022, the 11 objections over cracks "not included in the assessment of the damage", the three unavailable and three engaging a private valuer, the 17 members paid on 4 August 2022, the 15 households paid on 26 August 2022, the three water points finished by March 2023, the MWK 47 million estimate for the health centre at end 2023 and the promoter's figure of 22 new household connections by December 2023. The reports give no amounts paid for anything. The EIB loan of up to EUR 24.6 million approved in November 2016, the total cost of EUR 60.4 million and the Northern Region Water Board as promoter are all confirmed; the 15 December 2022 report does not give the signature date. The second complaint SG/E/2024/07 is a consultant's unpaid contract dispute, which the brief excludes.

dropped.candidate: eibcm:Tunisian roads and rail (S2 Sfax, Reseau Ferroviaire Rapide, Autoroute du Centre, G1, X4, S4 Zarzis, Sfax-Gabes)
dropped.reason: Cut from the draft. The one case written from this lead, rfr-bardo-expropriation-tunis, does not stand. The property at Bardo was never taken into possession, no compensation was ever paid, and the office found the compensation allegations not grounded. I read the conclusions report of 27 January 2020 in full, in two passes covering characters 0-100,000 and 99,000 to the end of its 112,012 characters (http://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2016-04-rfr-conclusions-report-en-27-01-2020.pdf), which closes the gap the writer left. The decisive point, which the draft missed: possession was not taken. Section 5.7 records the promoter awaiting execution of the decision to take possession, and the Court of First Instance dismissed the Public Prosecutor's demand to take possession on 26 June 2014. A later decision of 23 October 2017 concerned a challenge to an order of 17 May 2017 that possession should be taken; the court rejected the appeal on the merits but said it could not rule on the validity of the expropriation procedure. Nowhere in the report - and I looked specifically in the closing sections - does it say the land was occupied or used by the works, that the complainant lost the use of it, or that any compensation was paid. The promoter offered 250 dinars/m2 and then 400 dinars/m2; the complainant refused both and the file went to court. So the draft's title, "half a property taken at Bardo in 2014", is not supported: there is an expropriation decree of 7 January 2014, and the sentence "only half of the complainant's land was expropriated" is the EIB services' description of what that decree covered, which the draft turned into a completed land loss. What the office concluded is conditional or against itself. On compensation adequacy it found the allegation "not grounded in the context of EIB's obligations", said the amount offered in 2014 may be affected by elapsed time and inflation and that the project "may have a negative impact on the complainant's right on the expropriated land", and said the 2014 amount was likely inadequate only "if not addressed through a process of recalculation". Refusal to expropriate the remaining land was "not grounded" because the remainder exceeded the 25 per cent threshold; refusal to compensate in kind was "not grounded"; the cultural heritage allegation was "not grounded". The one grounded finding is stakeholder engagement, where the office found Tunisian EIA law lacks public consultation provisions and that this had "a tangible negative impact on the local ownership of the Project" - a finding about the Bank and the national framework, not harm to a person. The general observation that in Tunisia "the compensation amounts offered are very low and it is often necessary to go to court" is, as suspected, what EIB services told the office about the country, not about this complainant, and with the individual loss gone it would have been carrying the case. The counts of 31 expropriation procedures on line D in September 2016, 95 pending files in March 2015 with 69 referring to "land that is not in use at all", and 29 cases awaiting judgment in November 2018 are files, not people, and 69 of the 95 are on unused land. Verified and accurate as quoted but carrying no harm: the 2013 waiver (the EIB decided in July 2013 to conditionally waive the satisfactory Resettlement Action Plan condition for first disbursement, and first disbursement was made on 9 September 2013), the loan of up to EUR 177 million approved 21 October 2009 and signed 10 December 2010, AFD as leading institution with KfW and the European Commission (NIF) as co-financiers with no amounts given, the Bardo municipal council's unanimous decision in March 2019 on the temporary stop of works (reported by national press, and 16 council members resigned by the end of that month), and the recommendations with EIB services to report to the Management Committee during 2020 and the office to monitor by the first quarter of 2021. One draft quote was not verbatim: the court's reason reads "the first of the defendants, i.e. the first individual identified in the Expropriation Decree, was deceased". DEDUPE, as asked: this is not a duplicate of the existing case sfax-rocade-interchanges. That case is the Modernisation Routiere II road loan at the Sfax km 4 ring road, complaints SG/E/2018/43 and SG/E/2021/03, about 240 km away; this lead was the EUR 177 million Reseau Ferroviaire Rapide rail loan in Tunis, complaint SG/E/2016/04. Different project, different loan, different place. The question is moot now that the entry is cut. The rest of lead 24 - the five other Tunisian stretches - the writer dropped with the pages it opened, and those reasons are recorded in the lead_notes entry for lead 24 in this file. Drop upheld. I opened the dispute resolution report of 30 June 2025 (https://www.eib.org/files/complaints/2025-06-30PUBLIC-Disputeresolutionreport-SG-E-2024-27GreaterColomboWastewaterProject.pdf) and it records expected damage only. The 37 households of Narahenpita were concerned that the works "may cause damage to the surrounding houses" and "may cause land subsidence" near the site, and about "unpleasant smells", mosquito infestation and other health risks. The report records no actual damage to any house, no actual odour, no land subsidence and nobody actually moved; the agreed relocation is described as future steps, with residents to submit rental agreements and vacate after payment. Excavation for the Narahenpita pumping station began in September 2024 and the report says construction "generally progressed peacefully" after the October 2024 joint session, with completion planned for September 2026. The friendly solution entitles 23 owners of first-row housing units to a temporary relocation package of monthly rent for 12 months and transport costs, paid in four instalments; second-row residents are to be relocated only if structural stability is at risk, with minor damage repaired in place; and the promoter will coordinate with the Urban Development Authority on apartments for first-row owners, with assurance letters expected by July 2025, while saying it cannot guarantee relocation for interested second-row residents. All forward-looking, so test 2 fails. EIB financing confirmed: approved financing of EUR 50 million on 19 May 2016, finance contract signed 20 January 2017, borrower "the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka", promoter the Colombo Municipal Council. MERGE ANSWER, as asked. The EIB loan does NOT belong on the other agent's ADB case for project 36173-013. The dispute resolution report does not mention the ADB at all and does not describe the project as part of a wider programme, so it gives no basis for attaching the EIB to any ADB project. The EIB's own project sheet for 20140457 does (https://eib.org/en/projects/all/20140457): its description begins "As part of the Greater Colombo Water and Wastewater Management Improvement Investment Program", and the sheet says that programme was "initiated by the Asian Development Bank (ADB)". That named programme is ADB 45148, Greater Colombo Water and Wastewater Management Improvement Investment Program, which is a different and separately numbered operation from ADB 36173-013, the Greater Colombo Wastewater Management Project. The sheet also shows the signature as EUR 50,000,000 on 20/01/2017 plus a EUR 8,500,000 European Commission investment grant, EUR 58.5 million in total, against a total project cost of about EUR 156 million, and names no co-financing lender; it notes the ADB is conducting the initial environmental examinations for all components and that two components may require resettlement. The Early Warning System record for EIB-20140457 lists no co-financiers and no related ADB project number. So: if the other agent's case is on ADB 36173-013, the EIB should not be added to it as a lender on this evidence. The caveat the main session should weigh is that both are Colombo Municipal Council wastewater operations in the same city and the physical works could overlap on the ground; the separation here rests on project numbering and on the EIB's own statement of which programme its loan sits in, not on a document saying the two ADB projects are unrelated.

Drop upheld, and the quotation and the absence of a foreign owner both verified. I read the conclusions report annexed to the final reply (http://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2010-08-ecocimento-fibre-cement-moz-annex-1-public.pdf), page markers 2 to 11 plus an unnumbered closing run of sections 5.3.2 to 5.6.4 and the signatures. Section 5.1 begins exactly as the draft quoted it: "The Maputo site was not part of the Ecocimento Fiber Cement Project financed by the Bank," and the sentence continues that as a result no direct contractual obligations link the borrower and the Bank. Section 2.3 says "The decontamination operation in Maputo was dropped from the final Project Description", which covered only the Dondo site. The EIB loan was EUR 1.3 million from the Cotonou Investment Facility and financed Dondo. On ownership, the section 2.4 table gives Lusalite de Mozambique S.a.r.l. 95 per cent and two named individuals 2.5 per cent each, and section 2.6 says only "The Mozambican State has 20 % share in the Lusalite". No nationality or domicile is stated for Lusalite. I checked specifically for any foreign company, foreign owner, foreign lender or export credit agency connected to the Maputo site or to Lusalite and there is none. The only other entities named are the EIB itself, Banco Comercial e de Investimentos SARL as co-financier of the Dondo project and provider of a line of credit that temporarily eased Ecocimento's cash flow, MICOA, the Mozambican State, and general references to the European Ombudsman and the Maastricht Treaty; several parties including the guarantor, the investor, the complainant's company and the consulting occupational hygienist are redacted. The health harm at the site is documented - the occupational hygienist's report of 24 November 2008 found material "potentially polluting the environment and putting the workers and residents' health at risk", the MICOA audit of 27 July 2009 found "the existence of asbestos fibers, uncovered and exposed to the air, presented a risk", and the MICOA letter of 28 July 2010 described fibres "constituting a danger to the health of the local inhabitants" - so this would be a case if outside money or a foreign owner attached to the site. None does, and the office's own report says the site was outside the financed project, so the link test fails. One correction to the draft: it said the court injunction ordered "the seller of the site" to clean up the asbestos. The report refers to "a Court injunction against to clean up the asbestos" with the name of the party missing from the text, so who was ordered cannot be identified from it; section 5.6.4 says the complainant later pursued the matter in the national courts after obtaining the injunction.

Drop upheld. I re-opened the EBRD PCM annual report for 2011 (https://www.ebrd.com/downloads/integrity/pcm_annual_report_2011.pdf), which served normally. It records four complaints on the Tbilisi Railway Bypass received in March 2011: one from Mr David Chipashvili for Association Green Alternative requesting a Compliance Review, two from Mr Chipashvili for project-affected persons on the route requesting both functions, and one from Mrs Nino Saginashvili, a resident of the Avchala district. Twelve families in the gardening society of a former cognac winery in Avchala raised concerns including that the railway would "transport hazardous materials through their densely populated community", together with safety, environmental and health impacts, declining property values, water supply, visual impacts, difficulty communicating with the sponsor and getting project information, and who is compensated and resettled and who is not. Those are stated concerns, not recorded harm. The report says that on 4 November the project was cancelled and that "the Problem-solving Initiative was terminated on 7 November 2011", while the Compliance Review continued with Dr Bradlow starting on 12 December 2011. It records no land acquisition, house purchase, resettlement or compensation actually carried out at Avchala. One small correction: the report does not give the case numbers 2011/01 to 2011/04, so the lead's key cannot be confirmed from it. The draft's further findings - that the 2012 EBRD annual report says "No findings of non-compliance were made following the Compliance Review process", posted 23 July 2012, and that Bankwatch's project page carries the complaint and the financing but nothing on Avchala - I did not re-open, and they point the same way. Timing fails and no harm is recorded.
